newsitem.title: UK: British TV bans "offensive" anti-abortion ad.
newsitem.headline: British TV bans "offensive" anti-abortion ad.

text.p: British television networks on Tuesday refused to transmit an "offensive" anti-abortion election broadcast showing dead foetuses, provoking threats of legal action from activists contesting the May 1 general election.

The BBC said the election broadcast by the Pro-Life Alliance, a single-issue party with 56 election candidates, was "offensive under BBC guidelines and cannot be transmitted in the present form". Independent television network ITV also said the content was unsuitable for broadcast.
The Pro-Life Alliance said it would fight the decision.
"We reject this decision. We will be taking legal action on it in the High Court," a spokeswoman told Reuters.
"We're being denied our legitimate right of political expression to show the British public the truth about abortion," Bruno Quintavalle, director of the Pro-Life Alliance, told BBC radio.
But campaigners in favour of the right to abortion welcomed the decision.

"I am glad that these anti-abortionists will not be allowed to use this kind of emotionally charged material to mislead the public," Anne Marie Keay, chair of the National Abortion Campaign, said in a statement.
"The Pro-Life Alliance has no chance of winning any seats in the general election," she said. "They are only standing candidates as a ploy to gain airtime via a party political broadcast."

The broadcast was due to be shown on national television in Britain on Thursday. Any party fielding 50 candidates at the election is entitled to a five-minute slot on national television to advertise its policies.

The BBC said that a sequence of the proposed broadcast had been deemed offensive after "viewings with other broadcasters and careful consideration". But it said a Pro-Life Alliance radio broadcast, due to be aired on Wednesday, could go ahead.
ITV said the alliance was free to submit an alternative broadcast.
Opinion polls suggest the Pro-Life Alliance will win only a small percentage of votes in the election and has no chance of winning any seats.

A proposed election broadcast by the ultra right-wing British National Party has also generated controversy. Anti-racist groups have demanded that the broadcast be banned, but it has been cleared by BBC lawyers.
